# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

founder.order_why: Screen 14 (who else has to agree) belongs with screen 10 (who decides and pays), but the cost and price screens (12, 13) sit between them, so I answered the payer question, moved on to money, then came back to the payer question again.

founder.missing: My product is $599 glasses up front, then an optional $20/month plan, but screen 13 takes only one price, so I had to squeeze it into a yearly range. There was no place to say it is HSA/FSA eligible, which is how many buyers actually pay. Nothing asked whether a family member might buy it for the wearer, which my testimonials show (a daughter buying for her father). Nothing asked what the wearer needs in place to use it: a paired phone that is online, and English-speaking talkers.

PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 5 both ask what AirCaps is worth to me up front; the second is a follow-up, but it covers the same ground.
PRIMARY.missing: What I use today to follow conversations, such as live caption apps on my phone, lipreading, asking people to repeat, or an interpreter, and what I pay for those. screens.why1: Right after I said nobody besides the wearer has to agree, it makes sense to show me the list Keel built from that so I can check it before it becomes the belief.
screens.why2: The tags are plain, but the same person listed twice and the repeated heading 'The people involved' make me read it again to see whether Keel thinks there are two different people.
screens.why3: Who buys AirCaps is my own numbers: the wearer orders them, often with HSA/FSA money, and nobody else signs off.
screens.why4: Nobody else comes first and adds no invented role, but the wearer is split into two rows ('has the problem' and 'decides to buy') when they are one person, so two rows overlap.
screens.why5: It still says what I typed: the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree.
screens.why7: Nobody else is fixed first, Keel adds no role, and the belief (the wearer decides, nobody else agrees) matches my answer and can be supported or refuted; but the card says the person with the problem and the decider share one row where they are the same person, and here they are two.
screens.instead: The people involved — Nobody else · Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult · has the problem and decides to buy (add up to two who have to agree, up to 4 words each).

screens.why1: After I typed nobody else on the who-has-to-agree screen and checked it, confirming that this is the belief to test is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The belief reads plainly, but the bar's 'the last time they paid for something for this' stumbles, and the title packs two instructions into one long sentence, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: Whether my wearers decide and pay alone is something I know cold: HSA/FSA, the wearer orders, free returns.
screens.why4: The list holds only Nobody else, which is what I picked, so a single row to confirm is complete and correct.
screens.why5: It says the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides and nobody else must agree, which is exactly my answer.
screens.why7: A list holding only Nobody else is shown as a statement to confirm, the belief reads *nobody else* because I named nobody, and the bar counts decided alone as support, as the card requires.
screens.instead: Keel will test: the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else has to agree. It holds if at least 2 in 3 say they decided on their own the last time they paid for something like this. [Continue] [Go back and name who has to agree]

screens.why1: Right after I've set the price and said nobody else has to agree, asking what first step I want a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult to take is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint's examples, *pay for a pilot* and *let us run a trial*, are business-sales words; nobody I sell to runs a pilot, so I'd re-read to check whether a consumer order like mine fits.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want a wearer to do first: order the glasses on the 15-day risk-free return, and I can type it straight away.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in with a single *I'm not sure* chip, and that escape fits the founder side, since it leaves the dimension out rather than inventing a step.
screens.why5: My answer, *order the caption glasses with free returns*, is kept word for word with the free-returns term that defines it, and nothing in the screen changes it.
screens.why7: The box gets a step of up to 9 words in base form, but my step costs $599, and the screen never asks for the smaller free step the card requires when the step costs money, so the stranger's soft yes falls back to a bare *Probably yes*.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take, and what does it cost them? (e.g. "order the glasses with free returns", "book a free fitting"). If it costs money, what smaller free step would come first? (e.g. "a free try-on at an event")

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, it makes sense to show me how strangers will hear it before Keel tests it.
screens.why2: 'Order the caption glasses with free returns' is how I'd say it myself, and it is how our site sells it with 15-day risk-free returns.
screens.why3: Whether a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult would order a pair they can send back is exactly the decision my customers make on our site.
screens.why4: The step row reads well at 7/9 words, but the second row (6/9 words, presumably the free smaller step) is shown to me only as a word count, so I can't confirm it is the no-cost step I'd want.
screens.why5: Glasses, free returns and the act of ordering are all kept, so this still means what I typed, with no added timing, number or condition.
screens.why7: The step costs money (a $599 pair), so the card requires a smaller step that costs nothing; a second 6-word row appears to supply one, but I can't read it to check that it is free and is not the step again. The frame also says '5 of 5' where the registry puts commitment at order 6.
screens.instead: Show both rows in full: 'order the caption glasses with free returns' and a free smaller step such as 'a live demo of the captions', so the soft yes reads 'Probably, after a live demo of the captions first'.

screens.why1: Right after I set the first real step (order the caption glasses with free returns), deciding whether to ask strangers for it before the study goes out belongs here.
screens.why2: 'Pilot', 'leave your email' and the Pilot tab are plain to me as a YC founder, and the hint shows exactly the line people will get.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect emails from deaf and hard-of-hearing people willing to try the glasses is my own call to make.
screens.why4: Yes or No is complete and distinct for this decision, and no escape is needed.
screens.why5: The quoted line 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.' does not carry my step, ordering the caption glasses with free returns, so I can't tell whether respondents will hear what I actually asked of them.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you order the caption glasses with free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing an interviewer belongs just before launch, but for respondents who are deaf or hard of hearing, picking a voice to hear is an odd first concern, and the screen never asks whether the questions should lead with text.
screens.why2: Daphne, Saskia, the 5-second samples, 400 credits and the text-message link are all plain on first reading.
screens.why3: As the founder I can play both samples and pick one, and I know my people will mostly read rather than listen.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct, but the answer my respondents most need is missing: no option says captions or text first, with the voice optional.
screens.why5: My answer speaks of the face Keel preselects while the hint speaks only of a voice, so it is unclear whether the face, the voice or both are locked; nothing of AirCaps leaks to respondents.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? The text is always on screen and spoken aloud too; pick the face and voice (Daphne / Saskia), or choose text first with the voice muted unless they turn it on.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it makes sense to pick how my respondents answer before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Plain words: AI interviewer, read and tap, let them choose; I picked Read and tap at once.
screens.why3: I know my users and how they handle audio and video, so I can answer this from what I already know.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete as formats, but Daphne 'asks each question aloud' is an odd lead for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents, and there is no ASL or signed option for the Deaf respondents I also want to reach.
screens.why5: My audience is named correctly and nothing about AirCaps, the glasses or captions leaks into the choice.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or speak into boxes) / AI interviewer Daphne, every question captioned on screen / Let them choose, with a note that Daphne is captioned throughout.

screens.why1: After choosing how people answer, deciding who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain enough for a founder: people I know, a list from Keel's search, or one open link posted in a group; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen and reads fine at this point.
screens.why3: I know whether I am sending to deaf and hard-of-hearing people I know by name, from our community and waitlist, or posting in a group.
screens.why4: The three ways to reach people are distinct and cover my real choices; the open link fits a Deaf or HoH Facebook group or forum, and no escape is needed here.
screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name, is kept, and nothing of AirCaps leaks into the options.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits on the title line with the deciding count (1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month) right beside it, though I'd have expected Price at 0 of 7 to be the headline, not Existing sacrifice.
screens.why_b2: The tally (2 holding, 2 not, 1 not reached, 7 answered) and each card's 'bar 5 of 7' are plain, but the cards are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 under a '5 beliefs' count, and I had to look twice for the missing 5.
screens.why_b3: Price reads as my $599 plus optional $20 a month, but my Existing sacrifice was $200 to $1,500 a year in money people already spend on captioning, and here it is '12 conversations a month they lost the thread of', which I only recognise from the r25 rewording.
screens.why_b4: The status lines diagnose the problem ('they value it below your price', 'they lose less today than you estimated') but say nothing concrete about what to do, such as whether to test a lower glasses price or lead with the free plan.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, but 'they lose less today than you estimated' is stated as fact about my segment from 7 people with no low-n caution, and Commitment 'Holding up' at 6 of 7 sits beside 0 of 7 valuing it at $599 without the tension being flagged.
screens.instead: Not holding up on price: 0 of 7 valued AirCaps at $599 (bar 5 of 7), yet 6 of 7 would order with free returns. With only 7 people, re-ask at a lower up-front price or with the free-captions plan before changing the price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict is stated, Not holding up, smaller than you think, and the deciding number sits beside it: 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 counted, 1 for, 6 against and the marker at 5, but the unit reads 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month', which takes a second look to see what one cell counts.
screens.why_b3: I typed a money cost, $200 to $1,500 a year, and the card shows 'about 12 conversations a month'; only the loss phrase is mine, so the belief has been redrawn from money into a count.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the tally and points to the Price card, but it does not say what this means for my idea, such as not pitching AirCaps as replacing something they already pay for.
screens.why_b5: It says plainly that 7 is a lean, not a call, but it asks how many conversations 'fell through', which is not the same as losing the thread of one, and still concludes 'they lose less today than you estimated'.
screens.instead: Existing sacrifice: The problem already costs deaf and hard-of-hearing adults $200 to $1,500 a year. Ask 'Last year, about how much did you spend on captioning apps and hearing extras?' and say the result is a lean among 7, not a call.

screens.why_b1: The verdict reads 'Not holding up' and puts the deciding numbers right beside it: 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front, 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each.
screens.why_b2: Both ladders show counts per band marked for or against, my $599 and $20 are marked as band low edges, and the strip shows the bar at 5 of 7 with all 7 cells against, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The belief, $599 up front then an optional $20 a month plan, is my real pricing and I recognise it, but it is not the $599 to $839 a year range I typed in, so it is reworded.
screens.why_b4: The So line says where they clustered ($250 to under $599, 6 of 7) and points to Insights, but it never says what that means for the price, such as testing a lower entry price or leaning on trial pairs and free returns, which several quotes ask for.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than the answers carry; 'Fewer than 2 in 3' undersells a 0-of-7 result rather than overstating it.
screens.instead: None of 7 would pay $599 up front; 6 of 7 put it at $250 to under $599 and none would pay $20 a month. Before you lower the price, test whether a borrowed demo pair moves them, which several of them asked for.

screens.why_b1: The verdict *Not reached* sits right beside *0 of 7 named your price or more · nothing to ask*, and I see at once that this card decides nothing because nobody got as far as the money question.
screens.why_b2: Three bars all at 0 and a strip of 5 ghost cells, when 7 people answered, take a second look before I see that the chart is empty because nobody was asked and that the 5 is the floor, not 5 people.
screens.why_b3: The $599 up front and the optional $20 a month are my numbers, but *could find it in money they already spend on this* is Keel's derived belief and I never typed or checked it, yet the card labels it *Your belief*.
screens.why_b4: *Ability to pay waits until at least 5 do* tells me the card is blocked on Price, but it does not say what to do, for example that 6 of 7 sit at $250 to under $599, so the price or the price test is what to revisit.
screens.why_b5: No claim goes beyond the data: n=7 is visible, all 7 are listed as not asked because they named less, and nothing is called held or failed, though *Only 0 of 7* reads oddly.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of 7 named $599 (6 put it at $250 to under $599), so nobody was asked where the money would come from; settle the price first, then ask this.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 decided alone against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The four answers are counted over 7 people (6 for, 1 against), and the marker sits plainly at 5 of 7 on the strip.
screens.why_b3: It is my pick, Nobody else, on the wearer I named, though 'nobody else must agree first' reads a little awkwardly beside the bar line's 'nobody else has to agree'.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the tally and does not say what it means for me, for example sell straight to the wearer and lean on HSA/FSA, with no partner or family sign-off to plan for.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is a lean, not a call, but the So line flatly says 'They decide alone on purchases like this' for seven people, most of whom pay nothing today, which is one soft overstatement.
screens.instead: Most of the 7 (6) decided on their own last time, so you can sell to the wearer directly; one needed a spouse to agree, so a small group, a lean, not a call.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes and bar 5 of 7, so I know my belief held and by what margin.
screens.why_b2: Six for and one against out of seven, with the marker at 5, reads at a glance on the chart and the strip.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'order the caption glasses with free returns' are my own step word for word, though the rule line's soft yes ('probably, after try a pair of caption glasses first') is garbled and doesn't match the chart's 'Probably yes'.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is vague (book them into what: an order, a call, a waitlist?) and ignores that I just read 0 of 7 value it at $599, so it doesn't tell me what this yes is worth for the idea.
screens.why_b5: The screen does say 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the question named no price, so 'Book them into it' treats a priceless hypothetical yes as a sale after the Price card showed nobody at $599.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 said they'd order with free returns, but the question named no price and 0 of 7 valued it at $599; ask these six to order at $599 with the 15-day return and see who actually does.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Not holding up' with '0 of 7 at $599 or more, once · then: 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month · bar 5 of 7 on each' right beside it, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b3: It is my Price line, $599 up front and then an optional $20 a month plan, in the words I typed.
screens.why_b4: Apart from 'When a line fails · 1 min', the screen never says what this means for the idea; I have to work out for myself that people want to try a pair first and that I already offer 15-day returns they don't seem to know about.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 is visible, the one person who never saw the question (Amaka) is named, each group is shown as only 2, and nothing claims more than six people said.
screens.why_b6: I learned things I didn't type: people want to try before buying even though returns are free, they value hearing audience questions and many speakers talking over each other, a one-sided-deaf user gets by with seat choice, and most answers cluster at $250 to under $599 and under $10 a month.
screens.instead: Price failed 0 of 7, but most would pay $250 to under $599 and under $10 a month: put the 15-day free returns or a demo pair up front and show it keeping up with many voices at once, then test again.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it makes sense to check that I talk with hearing people before anything else is asked.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is the phrase we use ourselves, and the rest is everyday words I'd follow on first read or first hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I talked with hearing people this week, at work, in shops and with family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, they don't overlap, and a gate with no escape is right here.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's own segment words, and nothing about a product or company comes through to me.
screens.why6: One short question with a yes-or-no answer, easy to catch the first time the voice says it.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes; No

screens.why1: Once I've said I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea before asking about it makes sense, since this link has only the one part.
screens.why2: Captions, glasses and keeping eye contact are everyday words for me as a hard-of-hearing person, so I understand it on first reading.
screens.why3: Losing someone's face while I look down at a captioning app on my phone is exactly my life, so I can picture this right away.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It stays with the idea of captions in the lens of lightweight glasses, and there's no company jargon or talk of me as a 'user' or 'segment'.
screens.why6: It says well enough, but repeating 'lightweight glasses' and 'inside the lens' is padding to the ear, and 'When the people nearby are talking, you wear your lightweight glasses' sounds like I only put them on when someone talks, and that I already own them.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that captions nearby speech inside the lens. When someone talks to you, you see their words as captions in front of your eyes. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: After the idea card and the weekly-conversations screener, asking how often it already goes wrong for me makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: 'Fell through' reads to me like a plan collapsing, not like losing the thread or giving up on a chat I couldn't hear, so I'd have to read it twice to guess what counts.
screens.why3: It does happen to me, often weekly, but over a whole month I'd be guessing at a count rather than recalling one.
screens.why4: A box for the number, 'None' as zero and 'I can't recall' cover everything I could say, and they don't overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but 'fell through' is a vague stand-in for whatever the founder meant (conversations I couldn't follow or had to drop out of), so the meaning has drifted a little.
screens.why6: The question is short and says well, but 'A number of conversations last month' sounds like 'several conversations' rather than an ask for a number.
screens.why7: The box is on a single count-per-month measure and the one escape is there, but the verb is the vague kind the card warns against, and a month of conversations is a long window to count.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations with hearing people did you stop following partway through? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after the card about captioning glasses, asking what I'd pay for them makes sense, though the 'What you do today' kicker doesn't really match a price question.
screens.why2: 'Up front' and 'a month' are how I'd think about buying a hearing gadget and then paying for the captions, so I'd get it on first read.
screens.why3: I've priced hearing aids and captioning apps myself, so I can say from my own pocket what glasses like this would be worth to me.
screens.why4: Both ladders are complete and don't overlap, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is a real answer, and 'I can't say' sits apart as the escape.
screens.why5: AirCaps is named only because the idea card shows it on purpose, and nothing else of the company's plan or its own words for people like me comes through.
screens.why6: Each spoken step is one short question with four options I can hold, then a two-way pick, and the dollar amounts say cleanly.
screens.why7: This is one price first and then a plan, so it gets two six-rung ladders on price alone, each with a band edge at the founder's figure ($599 and $20), two bands below and three from it, 'I wouldn't pay for this' counted against, and 'I can't say' as the only escape.

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, asking what would make it worth more is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: It says my answer back as I'd say it, about $250 to $600 up front, and the question is short and plain.
screens.why3: I can say what would help me follow a noisy table, but I only know AirCaps from three lines on a card, so what would make it worth more is partly a guess.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was shown to me on the idea card on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or their words for people reaches me here.
screens.why6: One question and short, but "$250 to $600" said aloud is a mouthful of numbers before the question starts.
screens.instead: You said about $250 to $600 for AirCaps. What would it have to do for you to pay more?

screens.why1: Right after I said what I'd pay for AirCaps, it makes sense to ask whether I'd need anyone's say-so to buy it, though the kicker jumps from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself; I know straight away whether my partner or the insurance had a say last time I bought something for my hearing.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids, a captioning app and a loop system, so I know who had to agree, even if 'something like this' makes me pick which one.
screens.why4: The four run from me alone to someone else's call, cover insurance or family deciding, and 'I can't say' fits as the way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or their names for people leaks here; it's just about my own last purchase.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold by ear, though 'You decided on your own' read aloud as 'you' while the screen says 'I' is a small wobble.
screens.why7: With Nobody else tested, only 'I decided on my own' supports it and the other three refute it; the four are in the card's order, with the past forms, 'Someone else' in the second row and 'I can't say' set apart.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, the price and who else agrees, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the obvious last question of this part.
screens.why2: Ordering the caption glasses with free returns is plain to me on first hearing, since I've ordered hearing gear online before and know what free returns means.
screens.why3: I can answer from myself whether I'd order a pair to try at dinners and work meetings where I lose the thread, so it's my own decision, not a guess.
screens.why4: Yes, probably yes, probably not and no cover every answer I'd give, don't overlap, and the first one names the actual order, not a vague yes.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's step whole (order, the glasses, free returns), and nothing beyond the idea card I was shown reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard once, it's one short question and four short options I can hold, with no parenthesis, slash or abbreviation.
screens.why7: The first option says yes to the founder's own step and the soft yes is a yes to it too, with two answers for and two against, the four fixed answers in order, and no escape, as the card requires.
